abstract: The relationship between evolution and allostery is inherently intertwined. While structural studies have elucidated allosteric mechanisms, the extent to which evolutionary sequence information encodes these dynamic networks remains underexplored. Here, we introduce Sequence-based GNM-TE, a framework that integrates coevolutionary information with Gaussian Network Model (GNM) based Transfer Entropy (TE) calculations. This approach translates evolutionary constraints, shaped by both structural and functional requirements, into functionally meaningful allosteric dynamic information. Across 29 cases, we identify binding sites as dynamic hubs of collective information transfer and reveal mode-dependent, directional information flows between these sites. These findings overall indicate that evolutionary constraints embed the architecture of allosteric regulation within protein sequences, preserving binding site communication within layered dynamic ensembles that enable robust functional control and adaptation.

abstract:
Many RNA molecules function within confined environments, but the effect of confinement on RNA folding remains poorly understood. Proximity ligation experiments reveal altered long-range contacts in confined vs. unconfined states, yet they do not explain how spatial constraints give rise to these differences. Here, we develop a physical modeling approach that incorporates proximity ligation data into coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to reconstruct RNA 3D structures under confinement. We test our model on the
                    
                      
                        ∼
                      
                    
                    11 kb genome of the Zika virus, comparing the folding in virions (confined) and in cells (unconfined). We observe that the probability of contact between two regions of the genome vs. linear distance follows different scaling laws in the confined and unconfined cases, in agreement with proximity ligation experiments. We find that genome circularization—an interaction that regulates replication in Zika—occurs more frequently under confinement in both experiments and simulations. Our model reveals that the formation of long double-stranded stems through stacking confers local nematic liquid crystalline order to the RNA, and predicts pseudoknot topologies consistent with those seen in crystallographic structures of shorter RNAs. These results provide insight into the mechanism through which confinement alters the ensemble of 3D structures accessible to a long RNA molecule.

abstract: myo-Inositol trispyrophosphate (ITPP) is an allosteric effector of haemoglobin in vitro and has been proposed as a therapeutic agent for diseases associated with tissue hypoxia. Its surmised action on erythrocytes (red blood cells; RBCs) requires transmembrane passage and intracellular binding to haemoglobin; however, direct evidence, of the kind provided by 31P NMR spectroscopy, for entry of ITPP into RBCs has been absent despite proposed clinical use of the compound. We tested transport by monitoring fresh human RBC suspensions exposed to ITPP using non-invasive 31P NMR spectroscopy over several hours. No intracellular ITPP was detected within the sensitivity limits of the method (~ 30 µM), and no evidence of significant accumulation was observed. Neither was there evidence of its hydrolysis in haemolysates. We conclude that ITPP does not permeate the normal human RBC membrane in measurable quantities under the conditions examined (and realistic in vivo ones). Consequently, the reported effects of ITPP when added to suspensions of RBCs, on haemoglobin oxygenation are unlikely to result from direct intracellular interaction with haemoglobin and are more plausibly ascribed to indirect effects arising from perturbation of ionic equilibria (Donnan effects) that affect intracellular pH and membrane potential.

abstract: Magnetic Johnson noise--magnetic noise caused by thermal current fluctuations in conducting materials--can interfere with measurements and limit their sensitivity. As the sensitivity of experiments increases, it becomes increasingly important to accurately estimate the magnetic Johnson noise from experimental components with complex shapes during both the design and analysis phases. A particularly powerful approach is to combine the fluctuation-dissipation theorem with finite-element calculations. This versatile approach can be used to calculate the magnetic Johnson noise from conductors of arbitrary geometry for a wide range of frequencies and for magnetic field detectors with general geometries, such as a finite-sized loop or a gradiometer. Using a SQUID gradiometer array, we measured the magnetic Johnson noise from conductors with complex geometries and compared the results with calculations performed using this method. The calculations reproduce both the measured noise amplitude and its frequency dependence, providing an experimental validation of this method. We also performed a detailed analysis of how the geometry and material parameters affect the frequency dependence of magnetic Johnson noise.

abstract: Solvent extraction and drying of substrate-supported viscoelastic films and gels produce quasiperiodic networks of three-armed surface folds. In this Letter, we examine the physical mechanisms governing their formation, length scales, and geometric organization. We observed that swelling-induced compression in the pinned film drives localized folding of a stiffening, diffusively thickening surface skin over a drained underlayer. Combining experiments and theory, we reveal that both the pattern wavelength and fold-arm length scale with the dried-film thickness following a power-law with an exponent 5/8, with remarkably weak dependence on elastic modulus. The folds form 120-degree junctions on a triangular lattice, defining an open honeycomb network whose pitch satisfies p = sqrt(3)(aL + g), where g is the junction gap. Notably, the folds accommodate less than 0.1% of the stored compressive strain, implicating elastocapillary arrest, rather than strain relaxation, in limiting their amplitude. These findings establish distinct geometric, kinetic, and interfacial constraints governing pattern selection in drying soft solids.

abstract: We develop a stochastic Dean--Kawasaki field theory to predict the static structure factor and collective intermediate scattering function of interacting active Brownian particles. Starting from the microscopic overdamped dynamics, we derive coupled stochastic equations for the density and polarization fields using an angular-moment closure. Gaussian linearization then yields closed analytical expressions for static and dynamic density correlations in terms of propulsion speed, mean number density, interaction potential, translational and rotational diffusivities. The coupling between density and polarization predicts a crossover from exponential relaxation to damped oscillations despite the absence of inertia. For Gaussian-core potential, the predictions contain no fitting parameters. Brownian dynamics simulations show quantitative agreement at low activity and long wavelengths, and reproduce the crossover behaviour. For Weeks--Chandler--Andersen potential, the nonintegrable core makes both the Fourier transform of the potential and the self-interaction correction term in the Dean--Kawasaki field theory ill-defined. We therefore introduce an approximation that replaces the interaction potential with a passive direct-correlation function fitted separately at each density and temperature. This approximation requires no additional activity-dependent fitting parameters.

abstract: Within a hybrid quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics approach a small region of a large atomistic system is described quantum mechanically, while the rest of the system is represented by a classical force field. Despite this, the computational cost of the quantum calculation severely limits the accessible simulation and sampling time. Replacing the quantum calculation with a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on quantum reference data can greatly increase the accessible simulation time. However, the accuracy and efficiency strongly depend on the specific way in which the MLIP incorporates information about the classical (electrostatic) environment. Here, we demonstrate that existing strategies based purely on features derived from an external electric field fail to distinguish certain environments, ultimately limiting their accuracy. As a solution, we propose an extension to the equivariant TensorNet architecture that mitigates this shortcoming by incorporating classical atoms close to the quantum region into the message-passing scheme, combined with features derived from the electric field for describing the environment farther away. We show that this combination achieves higher accuracy than either approach alone.

abstract: The biotin-streptavidin interaction is a key component of nanobiotechnology, yet the nature of its cooperativity remains a debated question. Here, we introduce a label-free spectroscopy approach based on confocal UV autofluorescence microscopy to probe the binding cooperativity of this high-affinity system. By leveraging the intrinsic autofluorescence of tryptophan residues, we avoid artefacts associated with extrinsic fluorescent labels, enabling precise measurements of fully biotin-saturated streptavidin across a wide range of molar ratios. Our experimental results, supported by Monte Carlo simulations, provide conclusive evidence for the absence of cooperativity. However, we show that false signs of apparent positive cooperativity can emerge from local concentration inhomogeneities occurring when rapid reaction kinetics outpace mixing. By establishing the non-cooperative nature of biotin-streptavidin binding and identifying the key conditions to avoid cooperativity artefacts, these insights resolve a longstanding debate and offer critical implications for streptavidin-based biotechnological applications.

abstract: Macromolecular crowding is known to influence the diffusive, binding, kinetic, and equilibrium properties of proteins in a range of environments such as occur inside biological cells or in highly concentrated solutions of protein therapeutics. However a quantitative understanding of the effects of macromolecular crowding on the rates of protein-small molecule binding is lacking. Here, we present an adaptive model to simulate the association of two solutes in a macromolecularly crowded environment using Brownian dynamics and to compute the corresponding bimolecular association rate constant. The adaptive model represents interactions with atomistic detail for short-range crowder–noncrowder interactions, while using a coarse-grained approach for long-range crowder–noncrowder interactions and all crowder–crowder interactions. This multiscale approach is integrated in the Simulation of Diffusional Association (SDA) software for Brownian dynamics simulation of biomolecular diffusion. We applied this model to compute the rates of association for two contrasting protein-small molecule inhibitor complexes in environments varying in macromolecular crowder type and density, and we used Markov State modeling of the encounter trajectories to analyze the binding pathways. The results reveal competing effects: While the presence of the crowders can hinder ligand binding by reducing the translational diffusion rates of the solutes and obstructing the protein binding sites, crowders can also enhance the bimolecular association rate by other mechanisms, including channeling and the caging effect.

abstract: SUN-domain proteins are core components of LINC complexes that connect the cytoskeleton to the nucleus across the nuclear envelope. SUN5 is a testis-specific SUN-domain protein essential for anchoring the sperm tail to the nucleus, but its functional organization remained controversial, with previous reports suggesting that SUN5 represents an exception to the canonical topology of SUN-domain proteins. Here, we analyzed SUN5 organization during mammalian spermiogenesis using ultrastructure expansion microscopy (U-ExM), Tokuyasu immunogold labeling, and complementary biochemical assays. We show that SUN5 adopts a canonical SUN-domain protein topology at the head-to-tail junction and present a refined model of SUN5 positioning within the nuclear envelope. Stage-resolved U-ExM further reveals SUN5 redistribution including enrichment at the microtubule manchette and the perinuclear ring (PNR), suggesting additional roles in manchette-associated processes. Together, these findings clarify SUN5 topology and localization and provide a framework for understanding its function during mammalian spermiogenesis.

abstract: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a pivotal developmental program that is frequently co-opted to drive cancer aggressiveness and metastasis. While the dynamic remodelling of histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac) landscapes is a hallmark of EMT, the specific chromatin readers decoding these epigenetic signals remain largely unknown. Here, we identify ATAD2B as a novel H3K27ac reader essential for cell migration in both cancer metastasis and brain development. Multi-omics profiling revealed that, at EMT onset, ATAD2B targets H3K27ac at active epithelial identity genes via its bromodomain and recruits HDAC1 to epigenetically silence them, enforcing a mesenchymal state. ATAD2B loss impairs migration and invasion in breast cancer lines and Patient-Derived organoids, whereas its overexpression accelerates in vivo lung metastasis and correlates with poor patient survival. Furthermore, ATAD2B promotes the migration of newborn neurons in the developing brain. Our findings establish ATAD2B as a versatile chromatin reader orchestrating cell motility across development and disease.

abstract: In this study, we developed a computational model of a cell being stretched on a flexible membrane, a configuration that matches many in vitro experimental systems studying the effects of mechanical stretch on cultured cells. Using this model, we explored the complex patterns of stresses and strains present in the cell during dynamic stretching. We linked these intracellular stresses to a simple model of chromatin deformation to provide a rough estimate of chromatin reconfiguration resulting from nuclear strain. Together, this multiscale model of cell stretching offers a first-order approximation of cellular strain responses to dynamic substrate deformation. Our simulations identified an optimal range of applied strain that induces chromatin distention without causing cellular damage. This computationally determined optimal strain range aligns with recent experimental findings from our laboratory, where the same strain levels were shown to maximize nuclear localization of Yap/Taz and reduce senescence in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). These results provide a computational framework for understanding cellular responses to mechanical stimuli, potentially optimizing experimental designs and advancing the understanding of mechanobiology in stem cell research and tissue engineering applications.

abstract: Optimality principles are widely used to understand branching networks, yet they are tested on individual branchings that cannot reliably distinguish competing scaling laws. We formulate the missing link between the laws and measurements by mapping each law to its predicted branch points through global optimization. Vascular branch points closely match weighted-length optima when each vessel is allowed its own fitted weight. Inferred scaling laws reveal type-specific geometric signatures hidden from local analysis. They beat all tested laws, including Murray's law in 1,679 of 1,744 held-out hepatic and pulmonary trees. For coronary arteries on the heart surface, an exact discrete optimization model extends the framework beyond convex geometry and supports area-preserving scaling. The framework also identifies distinct laws for airways and plant shoots while rejecting weighted-length optimality for neuronal axons. Global optimization turns network geometry into a quantitative test of the principles that govern branching networks.

abstract: Melanoma cell migration is influenced by the expression of ELKIN1, an ion channel that supports mechanically-evoked currents when mechanical stimuli are applied to the cell-substrate interface, via the substrate. The deletion of ELKIN1 from melanoma cells impacts cell migration, cell invasion and cellular adaptation to changing gravitational loads. Here, we investigated whether ELKIN1 mediates calcium flickers at the cell-substrate interface as an indicator of channel activity, in the absence of externally applied forces. We found that calcium flickers can be detected in WM266/4 melanoma cells and that these flickers largely depended on ELKIN1 expression and acto-myosin contractility. Residual calcium flicker activity was detected in cells lacking ELKIN1, that was found to depend, in part, on TRPV4. However, this activity was not further blocked by inhibition of cellular contractility. These data suggest that ELKIN1 dependent signalling can be initiated by mechanical cues arising from cellular contractility.

abstract: Interferon-inducible protein 16 (IFI16) is a mammalian innate immune sensor composed of a filament-forming pyrin domain (PYD) followed by tandem HIN200 domains that bind nucleic acids. First recognized as a major regulator of inflammatory responses against cytosolic double-stranded (ds)DNA, IFI16 filaments have been implicated in several key mechanical processes involving both host and pathogens, including viral replication restriction, latency regulation, replication-stress responses, and DNA-damage responses. Moreover, IFI16 filaments are ultra-stable, a key trait believed to drive its autoantigenicity. Although recent studies reported that IFI16 undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) via disordered linkers and multivalent protein-dsDNA interactions, whether such a metastable entity provides a framework for the mechanical activities of IFI16 remains unknown. Here, we show that PYD-driven filament assembly confers the mechanical stability of IFI16 condensates by compacting DNA into ultra-stable tangles capable of withstanding forces sufficient to induce duplex deformation. By contrast, HIN200-dsDNA complexes are much more sensitive to ionic perturbation, DNA pretension, and mechanical interference. Together, we demonstrate that filament assembly allows IFI16 to act as a mechano-sensitive restrictor.

abstract: Homologous recombination (HR) is a critical repair pathway involving numerous proteins that ensure error-free DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) repair. Dysfunction in HR components can compromise genome integrity. Despite advances, many aspects of HR remain poorly understood. Notably, even one of the earliest identified and most critical interactions, between RAD51 and BRCA2, remains incompletely characterized, mainly due to the lack of structural data. This study presents a comprehensive biophysical analysis of the RAD51–BRC repeats interaction, integrating computational and experimental approaches. Starting with assessing the correlation between the binding affinities of individual BRC repeats and their impact on RAD51 disassembly, our investigation extends to larger BRCA2 truncations, offering unprecedented insights into the molecular determinants of RAD51 recognition. As mutations in the BRC repeats impair RAD51 recruitment and are associated with cancer, these results provide a valuable framework for interpreting pathogenic variants and guiding precision medicine therapies.

title: Breaking new ground into RAD51 BRC repeats interplay in homologous recombination

abstract: Mitochondrial Complex I generates reactive oxygen species at its flavin cofactor, where spin dependent reaction pathways have been proposed. Models of this chemistry treat the flavin oxygen radical pair in isolation, although the flavin is wired to a chain of eight iron sulfur clusters. Here we model the pair with this chain using the human Complex I structure and open quantum system models of spin coupling and electron transfer. In the simulated network, spin coherence decays rapidly along the chain, whereas proximal clusters alter the calculated radical-pair singlet yield. Their influence is kinetically gated: a downstream cluster affects the modelled yield when its electron-transfer rate competes with radical pair recombination, a threshold robust to driving force and to the transfer model. Modelling does set the sign: one directional spin hops predict suppression and inflate coherence transport, whereas charge resolved transfer drives the singlet yield towards its spin-randomized limit unless triplet recombination dominates. Detectable spin dependent effects in this framework require superoxide spin relaxation to be substantially slower than in free solution, a condition not yet established for Complex I.
authors: Sung, J.-Y.; Cheong, J.-H.
title: Kinetic gating by an iron sulfur chain modulates flavin radical-pair spin chemistry in mitochondrial Complex I

abstract: This paper discusses the applications of ultra-precision 3D printing in developing EPR sample tubes for X-band measurements of aqueous samples. The seed idea of this work started from the flat cell idea discussed in Mett and Hyde et al.(2003), Sidabras et al. (2005), and Sidabras et al. (2017), where placing multiple aqueous flat cells perpendicular to the electric field in the microwave cavity reduce RF losses and improve EPR signal sensitivity. In this work, we present the 3D printed aquastar sample holders for dielectric resonators and the aquasun sample holders for cavity resonators. Even though the ultra-precision 3D printing enables the fabrication of complex cross-sections at 25um resolution, the photopolymer material has comparatively higher dielectric losses compared to the conventional materials like glass and PTFE. To reduce the RF losses due to the inherent dielectric properties, we introduced the latticing approach in reducing the amount of plastic without compromising the structural stability. In addition to this, we present the slicing and dielectric approximation approach in reducing the computation cost for these complex cross-sections. The novel sample tubes discussed here present signal improvements through both simulation and experiments, which were validated through power saturation experiments. The sample tube development methodology presented here provide a general framework for designing and implementing 3D printed EPR sample holders, based on resonator electromagnetic field distribution and dielectric properties of the photopolymer material.
authors: Anilkumar, A.; Wherley, J. T.; Garces, A. M.; Lerch, M.; Klug, C.; Sidabras, J. W.
title: Ultra-precision 3D Printed Sample Tubes of Complex Cross Section for Enhanced Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Sensitivity of AqueousSamples

abstract: Conventional low-pass filters attenuate or remove high-frequency Fourier amplitudes but leave the phases intact wherever the amplitude response stays above zero. As a result, fine-scale detail of the original signal can persist beyond the target resolution. A sharp cutoff removes this detail but produces ringing artifacts. To address both limitations, this work introduces ramped phase randomization, which extends a conventional low-pass filter by adding random offsets to Fourier phases that increase smoothly with spatial frequency. For cryo-EM maps, the correlation between a map at the target resolution and an ideal, noiseless map sets the levels of the phase offsets, with a correction for the finite resolution of the input map. On three published map pairs, ramped phase filtering reduced the higher resolution parent's fine detail to a level similar to that of independently determined maps at the lower target resolution, whereas amplitude-only filtering kept the parent's sharp features. The FSCs between the filtered maps and their parents closely resembled those of the experimental maps. The same filter also serves as a data augmentation approach for neural network-based machine learning. With ramped phase randomization, each augmented copy keeps the power spectrum and low-frequency content of the original example but has a different high-frequency pattern. For simulated CryoBench particles of 16 ribosome assembly states, phase augmentation raised mean test accuracy in all 20 combinations of training-set size and latent dimension, by 20.8 percentage points on average (range from 3.3 points to 44.2 points). On two general deep learning benchmarks, mean test accuracy rose from 92.15% to 96.99% with 60 labelled UCI Synthetic Control traces and from 53.44% to 74.27% with 500 labelled noisy MNIST images. The ramped phase randomization is implemented in an open-source Python package, with a companion browser application for interactive visualization of cryo-EM maps and filtering effects.
authors: Dang, L. Y.; Jiang, W.
title: Low-pass filtering revisited: ramped phase randomization for cryo-EM map comparison and data augmentation

abstract: Single molecule analyses are providing new insights into the molecular mechanisms by which peripheral membrane proteins approach and translate across a target bilayer surface before stable docking. Here we compare and contrast the translational movements of four diffusers on a representative supported lipid bilayer: (i) the fluorescent lipid LRB-(DO)PE, (ii) the G-protein Rab1A anchored to (DO)PE; (iii) the PI(3)P sensor p40Phox PX domain, and (iv) the autophagy lipid kinase VPS34 Complex 1. The latter enzyme is a Class III PI-3-Kinase and its unusual architecture exhibits two distinct membrane-docking "feet" unique to Class III PI3Ks. Notably, the membrane contact surfaces of the PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase each possess multiple positive charges suitable for electrostatic interactions with their anionic target membrane. The present single molecule tracking studies reveal that both the fluorescent lipid and the lipid-anchored G protein Rab1A exhibit 2-dimensional translation typical of simple lipid diffusion in the bilayer. Single molecule density measurements indicate both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit significantly reduced membrane docking when the bilayer negative charge is decreased, confirming the importance of their protein-bilayer electrostatic interactions. Single molecule tracking studies reveal that both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit hopping movements across the bilayer surface during their initial bilayer contacts, yielding a significantly higher frequency of long range displacements than allowed by lipid 2-D diffusion. After transitioning from hopping to a stable bilayer-docked state, both PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase exhibit 2-D diffusion slower than lipid diffusion indicating the appearance of increased frictional drag against the bilayer due to new protein-bilayer contacts. PX domain requires its target lipid for the transition from electrostatic hopping to stable bilayer docking, while autophagy lipid kinase can dock spontaneously to anionic lipid bilayers even in the absence of its substrate lipid. In principle, the slowly diffusing, bilayer-docked states of PX domain and autophagy lipid kinase could be interrupted by unbinding-hopping-rebinding events. However, such events are not detected for PX domain in the presence of target lipid (DO)PI(3)P nor for autophagy lipid kinase in the presence of substrate lipid (DO)PI. Instead, unbinding-hopping-rebinding events are only observed for autophagy lipid kinase in the absence of substrate lipid, indicating that the presence of a specific binding lipid reduces the frequency or spatial amplitude of such events. Overall, the findings provide evidence that p40Phox PX domain possesses a search mechanism involving electrostatic hopping that speeds its acquisition of target lipid, as previously observed for PH domains. The evidence indicates that the autophagy lipid kinase also exhibits electrostatic hopping/skating behavior that is proposed to play a functional role by speeding regulatory encounters with autophagy lipid kinase activators and effectors. Moreover, the ability of the lipid kinase to spontaneously dock to anionic membranes without a target lipid could facilitate its distribution across broad regions of the growing autophagosome. Finally, the autophagy lipid kinase exhibits multiple translational modes that we hypothesize are enabled by its two membrane docking feet.
authors: Lizardos, L.; Ohashi, Y.; McCombs, A. M.; Knight, J. D.; Williams, R. L.; Falke, J. J.
title: Single Molecule Diffusion Studies Reveal Rapid Translations Across Target Membrane Surfaces for both p40Phox PX domain and Class III PI3K VPS34 Complex 1, the Autophagy Lipid Kinase

abstract: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is a large multi-protein structure that enables movement of macromolecules, such as mRNA and proteins, between the nucleoplasm and cytoplasm. There has been great interest in how the physical state of the NPC can influence nuclear-cytoplasmic transport. The hypothesis that the NPC may be mechanosensitive is supported by prior reports showing that the diameter of the NPC increases with nuclear envelope stretch as well as increased ECM stiffness. We therefore sought to develop a biosensor-based approach to determine if the NPC experiences mechanical tension.

abstract: Chiral symmetry breaking is a defining feature of life, visible at all scales from molecules to organisms. Yet how microscopic chirality propagates to shape the macroscopic properties of living matter remains poorly understood. Here, using a new experimental system of spinning microalgae, we show that a living chiral fluid behaves fundamentally differently from an externally driven one. As their density increases, cells self-assemble hydrodynamically into small rotating clusters which merge into a percolating chiral fluid. Strikingly, microscopic and macroscopic vorticity have opposite signs: individual cells all spin clockwise, yet clusters orbit counterclockwise. Combining experiments, theory and simulations, we show that both chirality inversion and percolation are direct consequences of the cells' internally driven nature. We then show how percolation reshapes transport, with even and odd diffusivities responding differently to the emerging network topology.

title: Chirality inversion and odd transport in a suspension of living rotors

abstract: We develop a nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic (VEP) model for the stress-strain response of metallic glasses by connecting the deformation dynamics with the material relaxation time obtained from independent stress-relaxation measurements. The material is modeled as a Maxwell-type element, with a nonlinear elastic spring and a stretched-exponential dashpot whose behavior is determined from the separate stress-relaxation data. The model captures the effects of temperature and strain rate on the initial elastic response, stress overshoot, post-yield softening, and steady flow. We independently determine the reference material-time function $X_0(\varepsilon)$ from the stress-relaxation response and the nonlinear material-time variable $X(\varepsilon)$ from the elastic-viscoplastic strain decomposition based on the stress-strain response. We introduce an Eyring-type function or material-time ratio $φ(\varepsilon)=X(\varepsilon)/X_0(\varepsilon)$ which quantifies the change of relaxation dynamics during nonlinear deformation. Our model provides a simple connection between structural relaxation and yielding in metallic glasses.
authors: Ankit Singh, Alessio Zaccone, Oleg Gendelman, Valeriy V. Ginzburg
title: Nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic model for the stress-strain and stress-relaxation in metallic glass

abstract: Local error correction can preserve classical information against noise, but protection under synchronized updates need not survive when sites evolve at independent random times. Establishing stability is particularly challenging when protection relies on the collective action of competing local rules. Here we develop a spacetime renormalization framework that reveals how independently acting local updates can collectively stabilize memory. We identify sufficient conditions under which the geometry of stable interfaces and suppression of defect propagation produce reliable erosion at large scales. Applying this framework, we prove stability of the asynchronous \textsf{R} squeezing code and introduce robust processes in two and three dimensions. In these systems, both encoded phases persist under sufficiently weak noise, even when the noise favors one phase. Our results provide a criterion for designing autonomous memories sustained by competing local stochastic dynamics.
authors: Shashwat Chakraborty, Jong Yeon Lee
title: Renormalization for Robust Memory without Synchronization

abstract: Tissue architecture is shaped by a variety of biomechanical and biochemical mechanisms, including morphogen patterning, differential growth, and spatial variations in cellular contractility. These mechanisms typically emphasize forces generated within cells. Here, we explore a complementary mechanism in which intercellular space itself exerts forces that shape tissue architecture. More specifically, we focus on hyaluronic acid (HA), a glycosaminoglycan of the extracellular matrix, that draws fluid into the spaces between cells through osmotic pressure, allowing these spaces to expand and mechanically deform the surrounding tissue. We propose that spatial patterning of HA-mediated extracellular forces, acting together with tissue geometry and junctional mechanics, provides a common physical framework capable of generating distinct tissue architectures. We test this hypothesis using a computational framework coupling a cell-based extended vertex model for biological tissues to a flow network representing HA and extracellular fluid in the extracellular space. This coupled model demonstrates a range of architectural responses spanning changes in tissue topology and morphology: global HA overexpression drives fluid accumulation and cell-cell junction rupture to produce multiple lumens in nontrivial patterns; a localized HA-rich region generates pressure gradients that drive budding; {\it multiple localized HA-rich regions generate branching;} and {\it extended HA-rich patterns can drive tubular structures.} Our results have direct experimental implications and establish the spatial patterning of HA-mediated intercellular forces as a mechanical morphogen helping shape tissue architecture.
authors: Kyungeun Kim, Brittany E. Schutrum, Claudia Fischbach, J. M. Schwarz
title: Hyaluronic acid over-expression drives tissue architecture in both healthy and diseased states

abstract: Food proteins play a critical role as emulsifiers, where adsorption at the oil and water interface governs emulsion formation and stability. However, quantitative characterization of interfacial protein load remains challenging due to polydispersity in conventional emulsification methods. We combine microfluidic generation of monodisperse emulsions with colorimetric protein quantification to measure the post-collection initial interfacial load ($Γ_0$) and subsequently monitored over 48 h to obtain the saturation load ($Γ_\infty$). Interfacial load exhibited a strong bulk concentration-dependent trend and was well described by a pseudo-first-order model. Both $Γ_0$ and $Γ_\infty$ followed sublinear scaling with concentration ($Γ_0$ ~ C^{0.21}$, $Γ_\infty$ ~ C^{0.12}$). Interfacial loads were largely independent of droplet diameter, with modest reductions in initial loading for the smallest droplets at low protein concentration. Measured loads exceeded idealized monolayer predictions and fell between bilayer and trilayer bounds, consistent with accumulation beyond a simplified monolayer model. Additionally, high-throughput mapping was performed across three proteins, seven concentrations, three pH values, and two ionic strengths, revealing that $α$-Casein exhibited higher interfacial loads than $β$-Casein and Whey protein Isolate, with maximum adsorption near the isoelectric point and at elevated ionic strength. In summary, this study establishes a quantitative experimental framework for linking protein properties, formulation conditions, and interfacial behavior using monodisperse microfluidic emulsions, while requiring only milligram-scale protein quantities.
authors: Varun Potdar, Alexander Favela, Michael Boehm, Stefan Baier, Siva Vanapalli
title: High-throughput quantification of interfacial protein load in monodisperse oil-in-water emulsions

abstract: Nematic liquid crystals confined in cylindrical pores adopt multiple stable director topologies --- radial, escaped, and arches --- each imprinting a distinct optical signature on transmitted circularly polarized light, with topological charge set by the projected director winding number, $\ell = 2m$. Using Landau--de Gennes and Jones-calculus modeling validated against micron-scale experiments, we show that this mechanism persists as the pore diameter shrinks toward the optical wavelength. However, full-wave Maxwell simulations of periodic sub-wavelength pore arrays reveal that the resulting vortex is a near-field phenomenon only: each topology imprints a distinguishable phase-singular signature --- differing in core multiplicity, core width, and ring amplitude --- directly below the pore array, but this signature does not survive propagation into the far field, where diffraction and inter-pore interference erase it within about one wavelength. Landau--de Gennes simulations further demonstrate that an applied electric field switches the pore between topologies, and hence between their near-field optical signatures. Because each topology is locally stable, sub-wavelength NLC pore arrays constitute an electrically reconfigurable, non-volatile platform for topology-encoded near-field optical readout, with potential application to optical labeling and anti-counterfeiting.
authors: Claire Doré, Brian Edwards, Nader Engheta, Kathleen J. Stebe
title: Multistable nematic liquid crystal pores as reconfigurable optical vortex metasurfaces

abstract: by Xiaohan Yu, Jing Zhang This study evaluates the agricultural co-benefits of large-scale environmental regulation. Existing studies often focus on crop yields and condition on production inputs that may themselves respond to policy interventions, potentially understating the overall production effect. Using Chinese county-level panel data from 2000 to 2024, we employ a reduced-form difference-in-differences (DiD) design to estimate the net total effect of the Air Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan (hereafter, the Action Plan) on per-capita agricultural output, with double machine learning used as a robustness check for flexible meteorological adjustment. The baseline DiD estimates indicate that the policy increased per-capita output of grain, vegetables and edible fungi, and oilseeds by approximately 42.6%, 10.4%, and 18.1%, respectively, in key regulated regions. Mechanism analysis shows that the policy significantly reduced fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations, consistent with the proposed biophysical pathway linking improved air quality to agricultural production. The reduced-form design may also retain production adjustments induced by environmental improvement, although these behavioral responses are not directly identified. Heterogeneity analysis indicates stronger grain responses in northern regions, whereas vegetables, edible fungi, and oilseeds show stronger responses in the South; grain and oilseed responses are also stronger in high-population areas. These findings provide evidence of agricultural co-benefits from air-pollution regulation and support closer coordination between environmental and agricultural policies.
authors: Xiaohan Yu, Jing Zhang
title: The agricultural synergistic dividend of environmental regulation and the identification of the net total effect: Evidence from China’s Air Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan

abstract: Lipid bilayer membranes can be solubilized in the form of disks of approximately 10 nm in diameter by several types of hydrophobic polyelectrolytes (HPE). The disks are stabilized by wrapped HPE along the rims of the disks. We compare the solubilization behavior of anionic HPE with chain lengths in between 20 - 100 monomers, and with varying molecular composition. We find that (1) HPE as short as 20 monomers can readily solubilize lipid bilayer membranes; (2) spatial intermolecular arrangement of ionic and hydrophobic groups in HPE determine if solubilization occurs; (3) anionic HPEs may exhibit two distinct pH-dependent solubilization transitions: the first is encountered in the lower-pH regime upon increasing the pH, whereas the second emerges at higher pH when the pH is decreased; (4) a binomial composition distribution of hydrophobic and ionizable groups over the chains, compared to a fixed composition, does not lead to a measurably wider pH range where solubilization occurs for the transition at low pH. We link the solubilization behavior of one of the HPE's to pH-dependent partitioning between macroscopic oil and water phases. Finally, (5) we find that linear composition superposition of the hydrophobic groups in HPE quantitatively accounts for the composition dependence of the pH's where solubilization occurs. This result holds within a range of compositions and breaks down below a critical fraction of hydrophobic residues in a HPE chain. Throughout, we compare the observations to a recently developed model for ligand-mediated cooperative transitions. Our findings have potential impact on anti-cancer medicine and drug delivery applications.

abstract: How much does a feedback controller need to know about the fluctuations it exploits? We address this question using a macroscopic information engine driven by self-propelled bristle-robots. Experimentally measured occupancy time series show that temporal correlations strongly affect vacancy detection. At short measurement intervals, mean first-passage times exceed independent-measurement predictions by more than an order of magnitude. A first-order Markov approximation captures much of this effect. It does not reproduce the full first-passage distribution, revealing higher-order temporal memory. Nevertheless, Markov-selected protocols come within 0.15\% of the maximum experimental power. Neglecting correlations causes power losses of several percent and favors larger compression distances. Introducing a sensing cost shifts the optimal strategy toward sparse sensing. The independent model cannot predict this shift, whereas the Markov model captures it. Cross-validation on separate time segments confirms the near-optimal performance of Markov-selected protocols. These findings demonstrate that near-optimal feedback control in correlated nonequilibrium systems can require a simpler statistical description than predicting their full temporal dynamics.

abstract: Using machine learning, we identify a second transition in polymer chain stretching driven by planar elongational flow, beyond the well-known coil-stretch transition. We achieve this by developing a conditional extension of Universal and Identifiable Dissipative Dynamics (UIDD) that jointly learns reduced stochastic dynamics from microscopic trajectories across flow strengths and yields the corresponding stationary nonequilibrium free energy landscapes. As the flow strength increases, the evolving landscape exhibits the expected coil-stretch transition, and then a previously unrecognized dynamical transition. In the latter, the stretched states persist, but the distribution along a folding coordinate becomes bimodal when conditioned on small end-to-end separation. Large-deviation analysis of a simplified analytical chain model reproduces both transitions and shows that they are phase transitions in the long-chain limit. Single-molecule DNA experiments provide qualitative support for the dynamical transition through the predicted reversal of the folding response.

abstract: Accurately predicting the transport properties of liquid electrolytes is critical for next-generation battery design and requires force fields that are both quantum-mechanically accurate and fast enough for long-timescale simulation. Recent large-scale pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approach density-functional-theory accuracy, but remain too slow to access the necessary timescales to converge transport properties. We provide a knowledge distillation procedure to transfer the accuracy of a large-scale "teacher" MLIP into fast, system-specific "students", without any additional ab initio data. Our distilled models run ~40x faster, reproduce teacher-predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days, rather than the months the teacher would require. Across a diverse set of sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions, establishing distillation as a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulations necessary for high-throughput electrolyte screening.

abstract: The accumulation of microswimmers near walls has been studied for decades. While hydrodynamics and single-cell kinematics are well-explored, the role of cell-cell interactions remains understudied. However, in realistic, crowded environments such as the human gut, these interactions can be just as crucial. Here, we demonstrate that they actively weaken bacterial surface accumulation. Analysis of entrapped cell tracks reveals that crowding enhances orientational fluctuations, which increase the effective rotational diffusion and facilitate wall escape. A minimal model shows that this collective effect is equivalent to raising the system’s effective temperature with density.

title: Crowding limits relative bacterial surface accumulation with density-induced effective heating

abstract: The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) signaling axis is a key effector of synaptic plasticity and neuroprotection. While TrkB activation is a major target to prevent neural dysfunction, stimulation with exogenous BDNF administration has not proven tractable given the unfavorable physiochemical properties of BDNF. In addition, BDNF also activates a cell death pathway by binding to the neurotrophin receptor p75. The TrkB agonist antibody ZEB85 provides an alternative route to the selective activation of TrkB. To understand the ZEB85 mechanism of action, we mapped the binding site for ZEB85 to the TrkB extracellular juxtamembrane domain and found a sulfotyrosine modification at residue 400 crucial for ZEB85 interaction and activation of TrkB signaling. We determined the structures of ZEB85 and BDNF bound to their respective binding sites on human TrkB suggesting independent sites for each ligand, despite prior evidence of direct competition. Using structure-guided BDNF- and ZEB85-binding deficient TrkB mutants, we assessed their ability to sequester ligands from full-length TrkB in cultured human neurons. We found that the BDNF binding site extends into the juxtamembrane domain of TrkB but does not require the sulfotyrosine 400 to activate TrkB. Together with biophysical analysis and AlphaFold modeling, these results explain how BDNF can displace ZEB85 from TrkB through an overlapping epitope. Our findings reveal unique features of TrkB, not present in the related neurotrophin receptors TrkA and TrkC and suggest future directions to explore the role of sulfotyrosine in TrkB signaling.

title: A sulfotyrosine motif in the human TrkB extracellular domain is required for activation by the agonist antibody ZEB85

abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.
authors: Huanxin Zhang, Weizhi Huang, Shihao Xu, Guy M. Genin, Xiangjun Peng, Xi-Qiao Feng
title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons

abstract: Clay films that dry on a rigid substrate crack, peel or stay intact, and which of these happens matters for coatings, barrier layers and ceramic processing. Composites of clay with polymers have been studied widely. Clay composites, whose components differ in size and charge, are much less explored. We show that mixing the nano scale clay Laponite with the micron scale clay Bentonite reduces desiccation damage on both a hydrophobic and a hydrophilic substrate, Laponite films stay essentially intact, Bentonite films fracture extensively, and on glass most intermediate compositions are less damaged than a simple average of the two would suggest. Rheology of the gelled suspensions reveals a two step yielding in every composition, and the cohesive energy derived from it depends by orders of magnitude on which step is used, a point that any rheology cracking correlation must specify. A dimensionless cohesion adhesion index, whose sign we derive from an energy balance, is consistent with compositions that peel on polypropylene and crack on glass. Replicate experiments were performed for robustness of results. The results identify composition as a simple handle on the crack resistance of clay films and open the search for the critical crack-free thickness as a function of clay composition.
authors: Tapati Dutta, Agnishikha Chakrabarti, Soham Mitra, Deepshikha Das, Indranil Chakraborty
title: Resisting Drying Stress in Laponite Bentonite Clay Composites, Two Step Yielding and Crack Peel Selection

abstract: In this study, we investigate the waiting time dependence and the protocol dependence of thermally activated events in structural glasses using molecular simulations and potential energy landscape analysis. We find a qualitative crossover in the nature of activation events; from avalanche-like events to local events. We also use the isoconfigurational ensemble analysis and reveal that the events become less diverse and more reversible. We discuss these crossovers from the perspective of the stability and the potential energy landscape of glasses. To investigate the protocol dependence, we compare the two types of glasses whose stability is controlled by waiting time and parent temperature, respectively. Surprisingly, at the same inherent structure energy level, the parent-temperature-controlled glasses are more unstable and maintain their avalanche-like nature. These results demonstrate that the activation properties of structural glasses are not determined solely by their energy levels, highlighting the essential role of state connectivity and the dynamical sampling in the complex energy landscape.
authors: Yuki Takaha, Atsushi Ikeda
title: Aging and protocol dependence of thermal activation events in structural glasses

abstract: Rotary molecular motors commonly couple components with different rotational symmetries, but how this gearing controls energy transduction remains unclear. Here we show that symmetry can produce a fundamental tradeoff in coupled stochastic barrierless rotary motors: the gear ratio that maximizes output power under tight coupling is also the ratio that requires the strongest coupling to remain locked. Consequently, weakening the coupling can invert the effect of gearing, transforming a power maximum into a local minimum. At strong driving, both the power-optimal and most slip-susceptible ratios approach symmetry match. Numerical solutions of the Fokker-Planck dynamics for rotors with finite energy barriers reproduce these predictions and reveal how the behavior changes when driving strength is fixed per rotation or per subunit. Motivated by the bacterial flagellar motor, these results identify coupling strength as a key determinant of whether matched rotational symmetries enhance or suppress energy transduction, providing a general design principle for coupled molecular motors.
authors: Sara Iranbakhsh, David A. Sivak
title: Two faces of symmetry match in gear-like coupled rotary motors

abstract: The ideal glass transition has often been associated with the extrapolated vanishing of configurational entropy $S_c$, yet how this thermodynamic criterion is reflected in microscopic dynamics remains unclear. Here, we show that the vanishing of deterministic chaos quantified by the maximum Lyapunov exponent $λ_{\mathrm{max}}$ provides such a dynamical signature. Using molecular dynamics simulations across diverse model glass-forming liquids in two and three dimensions, we show that $λ_{\mathrm{max}}$ follows an approximate scaling $λ_{\mathrm{max}} \propto (T-T_λ)^{1/2}$ and extrapolates to zero at a temperature $T_λ$ consistent with the Kauzmann temperature $T_{\mathrm{K}}$. Furthermore, we establish the quantitative relation $λ_{\mathrm{max}}^2 \propto T S_c$, directly linking chaotic dynamics to configurational entropy. By demonstrating that $λ_{\mathrm{max}}^2 \propto σ_K^2$, where $σ_K^2$ is the variance of local potential energy landscape curvature fluctuations, we connect the suppression of chaos directly to landscape geometry. These results provide a unified thermodynamic, dynamical, and geometric framework for glass formation, identifying the ideal glass transition as the endpoint of chaotic exploration of the energy landscape.
authors: Zi-Long Wang, Jack F. Douglas, Matteo Baggioli, Zhao-Yan Sun, Wen-Sheng Xu
title: The End of Chaos at the Ideal Glass Transition

abstract: Cells experience epigenetic, osmotic, and mechanical perturbations that reorganize chromatin, yet how these distinct cues are integrated into a common physical response of the nucleus remains unclear. Here, we identify nuclear hydration as a central state variable that links microenvironmental perturbations to chromatin phase organization and nuclear mechanics. We develop a non-equilibrium mesoscale model that couples chromatin elasticity, water transport, and epigenetic reaction-diffusion kinetics. In this framework, chromatin behaves as a deformable polymer that segregates into coexisting water-rich euchromatic and water-poor heterochromatic phases, whose compositions and morphologies are regulated by hydration-dependent swelling, elastic strain, and histone-mark interconversion. The model predicts that epigenetic perturbations, osmotic shocks, and volume-changing mechanical loads reorganize chromatin by shifting intranuclear water content, nuclear volume, and euchromatin-heterochromatin phase balance. It further predicts that anisotropic forces impose directional strain, driving heterochromatin elongation, alignment, and lamellar transitions. Quantitative comparisons with super-resolution imaging, AFM and chromatin-accessibility measurement - across pharmacological, osmotic, and mechanical perturbations including confinement and micropatterning - support these predictions. Together, our results establish a chemo-mechano-osmotic framework in which nuclear hydration integrates biochemical and biophysical cues to regulate chromatin organization across scales.

title: Osmotic Coupling of Mechanics and Epigenetics Regulates Chromatin Phase Organization

abstract: Mitochondrial networks are shaped not only by fission and fusion but also by mechanical forces. Here, we examine pulling-induced branch formation and contrast it with fusion-based branch formation. Live imaging reveals that branches formed by pulling are shorter-lived but initiate more frequently and with a narrower range of angles, concomitantly inducing deformation in parent mitochondria – in contrast with those formed by fusion. In addition, perturbations to microtubule stability and motor protein association with mitochondria alter pulled branch lifetimes, emphasizing the role of cytoskeletal dynamics in branch stability.
authors: Sheda Ben Nejma, Rajit Narayanan Cheramangalam, Juan C. Landoni, Matthew D. Lycas, Julius Winter, Moumita Das, Suliana Manley
title: A Biophysical Framework for Force-Induced Mitochondrial Branches

abstract: Among the various clock genes, Cryptochromes have been identified as pivotal constituents of the molecular clock regulating the circadian rhythm. Evidence suggests that physical activity exerts an impact on both the circadian rhythm and the sleep quality. In this regard, this study aimed to assess the effects of multi-component exercise program (MCEP) on circadian protein regulation and sleep quality in healthy and non-active females. A total of twenty-two untrained young women (18–40 yrs), were randomly assigned to two parallel groups: exercise (EXE; n = 11; BMI = 22.23 ± 2.19 kg/m2; Age = 26.09 ± 4.88 years) and control (CON; n = 11; BMI = 23.57 ± 2.79 kg/m2, Age = 29.09 ± 6.3 years) using simple randomization. Outcome assessors were blinded to group allocation. The EXE group implemented a (MCEP) consisting of moderate-intensity aerobic exercises, resistance exercises, and balance exercises for 3 consecutive days. The study was conducted over 4 days and 3 nights by measuring Cryptochrome1 protein (CRY1), sleep quality, blood pressure, heart rate, and body temperature at 08:00, 00:00, and 18:00. This study was conducted at the sports complex and guesthouse of the Faculty of Physical Education at Allameh Tabataba’i University. Results showed there was no significant relationship between the CRY1 levels and Sleep quality (r= -0.36, p = 0.123). Moreover, (MCEP) had no significant effect on the serum level of CRY1 (p = 0.144). Overall, in other measurements, a significant difference was observed in heart rate (HR) within the EXE group (p = 0.001, effect size = 0.27 (0.3% decreased)), and in systolic blood pressure (SBP) within the CON group (p = 0.001, effect size = 1(9% increased)). Conversely, there is a significant decrease in diastolic blood pressure (DBP) in the EXE group when compared to the CON group (p = 0.009, effect size = 0.91). However, in the sleep quality index, the subjective sleep quality in the EXE group significantly increased (p = 0.039, effect size = 0.55 (122% increased)), and sleep latency showed a significant decrease in the CON group (p = 0.021, effect size = 0.55 (50% decrease)). In this study, aerobic training (AT) was conducted at up to 60–70% of HRmax for 30 min, while resistance training (RT) lasted 20 min. Future research could extend (AT) duration to 40 min or adjust the intensity (e.g., 65–75%), incorporate other equipment (e.g., weight) in (RT) with increased repetitions and sets, and extend the overall exercise duration to 90 min. Additionally, future studies should focus on long-term adherence to optimize benefits. The trial was registered with the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT) under registration number [IRCT20260722070304N1]. The trial record is available at [https://en.irct.ir/trial/92016].
authors: Tartibian, Bakhtyar, Akbarizadeh, Samaneh, Eslami, Rasoul
title: Impact of a multi-component exercise program on circadian protein regulation and sleep quality in healthy females: a randomized controlled trial

abstract: When cells collide, they often exhibit “contact inhibition of locomotion” (CIL), a behavior in which cells repolarize and migrate away from the site of contact. Experimental CIL outcomes are highly variable—why? Here, we develop a minimal stochastic model to quantify how intrinsic noise in cell polarity, arising from the finite number of signaling molecules, influences CIL decision-making. We simulate polarization dynamics by tracking individual Rho GTPase proteins that diffuse and switch stochastically between the cell membrane and cytosol.
authors: Mariia Kryvoruchko, Brian A. Camley
title: Intrinsic stochasticity in cell polarity and contact inhibition of locomotion

abstract: Collisionless shocks are among the most efficient particle accelerators in the Universe, yet the physical mechanism responsible for energetic upstream seed ions remains poorly understood. Using two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations of unmagnetized relativistic electron-ion shocks, we investigate ion pre-acceleration by self-generated magnetic dipole vortices (MDVs) in the upstream region of the shock. We identify two distinct ion populations: one remains phase-matched with the moving MDV, undergoes considerable energization, and returns toward the shock, whereas the other escapes upstream after gaining only modest energy. We show that the magnetic component of the Lorentz force reduces the ion’s longitudinal velocity relative to the moving MDV, extending the interaction time and allowing the transverse electric field to perform sustained positive work. Decomposition of the electric field shows that both the motional electric field associated with the moving MDV and plasma-generated fields contribute to the observed ion energization. Repeated interactions with successive MDVs can increase ion energy before the particles return to the shock transition region. These results identify MDV-mediated upstream ion pre-acceleration as a candidate mechanism for producing energetic seed ions that may facilitate subsequent shock acceleration.
authors: Naseri, Neda, Turkakin, Hava, Shvets, Gennady
title: Phase-matched ion pre-acceleration by upstream magnetic dipole vortices in relativistic collisionless shocks

abstract: Guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs) defend host cells by assembling on intracellular pathogen membranes. For human GBP1, this requires a switch from a compact, closed conformation to an extended, open one, whereas for murine orthologues the open state is not known. How the open state behaves at a membrane has remained inaccessible to experiment. Using all-atom and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations covering over 0.5 ms, we followed human GBP1 and murine GBP2 as monomers, dimers, and higher-order assemblies on phosphatidylcholine membranes, Shigella flexneri lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and phosphoinositide-containing bilayers. Closed GBPs dock through their prenyl anchor with minimal lipid selectivity. Open GBPs, by contrast, are intrinsically unstable: monomers fold back into membrane-bound resting states, and dimers tip over unless supported, either by long LPS O-antigen chains or by neighboring molecules within a coat. The open state thus appears to be maintained not by the nucleotide alone but by the protein's molecular environment.
authors: Bundschuh, B. F.; Loschwitz, J.; Strodel, B.
title: Lipopolysaccharide chain length and coat assembly keep guanylate-binding proteins upright on bacterial membranes

abstract: Gut bacteria experience a spatially structured environment with hydrodynamic flow. Using a branching-process approach, we show that beneficial mutants arising randomly upon division have a reduced fixation probability compared to the well-mixed case. The suppression factor is set by the spatial heterogeneity of mutant fate across the gut. In contrast, the invasion of mutant lineages that avoid early stochastic extinction is accelerated in the gut compared to a matched well-mixed case. Stronger advective flow decreases fixation probabilities while accelerating mutant invasion.
authors: Alexandre, A.; Loverdo, C.; Bitbol, A.-F.
title: Hydrodynamic flow in the gut hinders the fixation of beneficial mutants but accelerates their invasion

abstract: Philadelphia chromosome positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL) is the most common genetic subgroup in adult ALL, and its incidence increases with age. In this longitudinal single-subject study, we investigate erythrocyte deformability as a disease-associated biomechanical marker in parallel with clinical, hematological, and molecular response throughout the treatment process in a 75-year-old patient diagnosed with Ph+ ALL. Using optical tweezers, we performed high-resolution single-cell mechanical stretching experiments to quantify the deformability of individual RBCs obtained from the patient and a healthy control. Our measurements reveal a pronounced relation between state of diseases/therapy and RBC deformability in the ALL patient, indicating systemic alterations in cellular biomechanics associated with leukemic pathophysiology. These findings suggest that changes in RBC mechanical properties, probed through non-invasive optical tweezers-based techniques, may accompany disease presence and progression.
authors: Pesen, T.; Koc, Y.; Bagislar, B. B.; Alhan, N.; Akgun, B.
title: RBC Deformability During Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment

abstract: Single-molecule total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy provides unparalleled insight into biological processes, but reaches fundamental limits due to the challenges of imaging individual fluorophores, where limited photon counts mean signals often border background noise. Practically, trade-offs exist between emission rate, time resolution, and observation lifetime. Experimentalists increasingly seek higher time resolution and longer observational times, demanding accurate quantification of fluorescence intensity and super-resolved positional information.
authors: Aref Enayati, Hannah M. Baird, Mathias S. Weyland, Alke Petri-Fink, Marco Lattuada, W. David Jamieson, Rudolf Marcel Füchslin, Oliver Castell
title: Enhanced Quantitative Accuracy in Single Molecule Imaging: A Fidelity-Guided Denoising Approach

abstract: Viral surface glycoproteins function within crowded, membrane-anchored supramolecular assemblies, yet their dynamics are often inferred from soluble, engineered ectodomains. For SARS-CoV-2 Spike (S), this distinction is especially important because variant mutations evolved in the context of intact virions, not engineered trimers. Here, we combined cyclic ion mobility mass spectrometry (CIM-MS) for hydrogen deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDXMS) with computational weighted ensemble molecular dynamic (WE-MD) simulations to compare the conformational effects of SARS-CoV-2 mutations in two S protein constructs: soluble recombinant 2P S and full-length S displayed in virus-like particles (VLPs).

title: Supramolecular assembly and membrane anchoring alter variant-induced SARS-CoV-2 Spike conformational dynamics

abstract: Internal degrees of freedom of cross-linked polymer networks enable compressible hydrogels and microgels to swell or deswell by absorbing or expelling solvent in response to environmental changes. Macromolecules in solution can influence the swelling response by acting as crowding agents, with practical relevance for drug delivery and biosensing. We extend the Flory-Rehner theory of polymer network swelling to incorporate nanoparticle crowders as another implicit species that can perturb a gel through volume exclusion, including the entropic cost of crowder penetration from polymer field theory. Within the free energy landscape of asymmetric ternary mixtures, we numerically solve equilibrium relations equating solvent and crowder chemical potentials inside and outside the gel. Independently, we perform Monte Carlo simulations, including trial moves that allow gels to swell and take up crowders. We investigate how crowder size, solution concentration, cross-link density, and solvent quality influence swelling of polymeric gels, partitioning of crowders between inside and outside, and structural properties of microgel suspensions governed by Hertzian elastic pair interactions. Our results show that nanoparticle crowding promotes deswelling, thereby weakening interparticle correlations, and that, with increasing the concentration of crowders, polymeric gels reach a maximum loading capacity, dependent on crowder size and polymer cross-link density.
authors: Mahesh Aryal, Alan R. Denton
title: Response of Hydrogels and Microgels to Nanoparticle Crowding

abstract: Nonreciprocal interactions are a generic source of nonequilibrium dynamics, yet their consequences for nematic topological defects remain unexplored. We introduce a nonreciprocal nematic model on a two-dimensional hexagonal lattice and formulate a continuum theory containing a nematic nonreciprocal torque. In the deterministic limit, simulations and symmetry analysis show that this torque drives +1/2 defects to self-propel along their polar axes. Nonreciprocity modifies the splitting pathway of integer +1 defects. These results identify a symmetry-resolved route from nonreciprocity to nematic defect transport and topological reorganization, distinct from active-stress-driven motion.
authors: Yunpeng Cao, Yu Du, Yao Li
title: Nonreciprocity Propels Nematic Defects

abstract: We study the mean first-reaction time (MFRT) of a Brownian particle in a bounded three-dimensional domain $Ω$ with a reflecting boundary $\partialΩ$, that contains a thin reactive filament. The filament is a tube of cross-sectional diameter $\varepsilon\ll 1$ around a smooth closed curve $Γ$, and its surface is partially reactive with reactivity $b$. As $\varepsilon\to 0$ the filament reduces to a line source in the outer problem. Its cross-section enters only through a logarithmic reactive capacitance $d_c(b)$, so that the MFRT is O$(-\log[\varepsilon d_c])$. This contrasts with the $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ scaling for spatially localized traps of radius $\varepsilon$. Using matched asymptotic expansions, we derive a Fredholm integral equation on $Γ$ for the line density of the reactive flux. It sums all powers of $ν\equiv -1/\log[\varepsilon d_c]$ and involves two geometric quantities: the regular part $R$ of the Neumann Green's function, which encodes the interaction of $Γ$ with $\partialΩ$, and an intrinsic self-energy of $Γ$ that depends only on its shape. The framework extends to multiple filaments, splitting probabilities, a spatially heterogeneous diffusivity, and the principal eigenvalue of the Laplacian. For the unit sphere we solve the integral equation with a simple trapezoidal Nyström scheme, and we validate the predictions for rings, linked rings and torus knots against full 3-D finite-element solutions.
authors: Denis S. Grebenkov, Theodore Kolokolnikov, Alan E. Lindsay, Michael J. Ward
title: The Mean First-Reaction Time on a Thin Filament in a 3-D Domain

abstract: The dynamics and stability of a swarm of microswimmers is examined here using a thermodynamically compliant microswimmer model. The theory presented here is a mean-field model in which the swarm is considered to be a uniform solution of swimmers that are moving, on average, in the same direction. The hydrodynamic interaction between swimmers is modeled accurately assuming a crystalline arrangement to the swarm. A swimmer in the swarm can swim up to twelve times faster than when alone in an infinite sea, when the volume fraction of swimmers in the swarm is about 0.14. Moreover we have also studied the stability of the swarm around a uniform crystalline arrangement by calculating the hydrodynamic torques generated by the swarm as a function of the volume fraction of swimmers. The predictions presented here agree with recent multiparticle simulations that have shown that hydrodynamic torques have a stabilizing effect in swarms of pullers while swarms of pushers are generally destabilized by hydrodynamic interactions. The thermodynamically admissible coupling between the swimmer's motion and fuel consumption allows us to study the full dynamics instead of artificially constrained steady-states only. By accounting for fuel consumption and high order hydrodynamic interactions we are able to examine the swarm's stability as function of fuel concentration and the volume fraction of swimmers. We find that at high concentrations of fuel, swarms of pullers are stabilized by hydrodynamic torques for volume fractions of swimmers as low as 0.02 but at lower volume fractions Brownian forces make the swarm unstable.
authors: Andrés Córdoba, Jay D. Schieber
title: The effects of hydrodynamic interactions on the swimming velocity and stability of a swarm of microswimmers

abstract: by Erika Yamauchi, Hayato Fujita, Yukari Miyake, Kaneyoshi Yamamoto Bacteria rapidly initiate growth when entering warm-blooded hosts to ensure reproductive success. We investigated the temperature-dependent stimulation of the specific growth rate at the onset of the logarithmic phase (defined as μ at ODratio = 0.2) in Escherichia coli. High-frequency automated monitoring revealed that this stimulation peaks near 37°C and is strain-specific. Comparative analysis between MG1655 and W3110 type A identified the Rac prophage as a primary genomic determinant for this acceleration. However, growth stimulation is uniquely dependent on H-NS, which we redefine as a nucleoid structural organizer. Genetic complementation and comparative analysis of nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs), and single-cell nucleoid imaging confirmed that H-NS provides a mandatory physical scaffold specifically at host temperatures. We propose that H-NS undergoes a conformational switch to a parallel dimer form around 37°C, enabling the nucleoid to adopt the highly condensed state required for managing replication-transcription conflicts during rapid growth bursts. Notably, while MG1655 relies primarily on H-NS for this stimulation, W3110 type A requires a distributed network of NAPs, including HU and StpA, to maintain its growth velocity. This effect is environment-specific, becoming particularly significant under minimal media conditions where metabolic and structural coordination requirements are more stringent, but less pronounced in nutrient-rich conditions. These findings resolve the silencing paradox: hns-deficient mutants grow slowly at 37°C because they lack the structural infrastructure required to physically coordinate the rapid onset of growth, regardless of the de-repression of growth-promoting genes. We conclude that H-NS-mediated physical organization of the genome is a fundamental prerequisite for temperature-dependent growth adaptation and successful host colonization.
authors: Erika Yamauchi, Hayato Fujita, Yukari Miyake, Kaneyoshi Yamamoto
title: Structural basis of H-NS-mediated temperature-dependent stimulation of initial growth in Escherichia coli

abstract: A major question in active matter is how interactions between particles are modified by activity. Here, we address this question for Coulomb interactions by considering a charged swimmer immersed in an electrolyte. A static charge is screened by an ionic cloud that decays over the Debye length $λ_D$. We show that the persistent motion of the swimmer can qualitatively modify the steady-state ionic charge-density profile. At low activity, the swimmer appears effectively quasistatic to the ions, and conventional Debye-Hückel screening is recovered. At higher activity, the ballistic-to-diffusive dynamics of the swimmer are reflected in distinct spatial regimes. A power-law decay is followed by a stretched-exponential decay at intermediate distances. At sufficiently large distances, exponential screening is restored, but with an increased screening length, $λ>λ_D$, revealing activity-induced underscreening. Thus, active motion modifies both the spatial form and the range of electrostatic screening. Our results motivate the study of active electrolytes composed of positively and negatively charged swimmers.
authors: Tanmoy Chakraborty, Tomer Markovich, Ram M. Adar
title: Swimming versus Screening: How Activity Reshapes the Ionic Cloud of a Charged Particle

abstract: Soft composites, materials consisting of inclusions within a polymeric matrix, offer a broad design space with diverse mechanical properties. Composite stiffness is normally set by the volume fraction of filler, and classical theory predicts at most ~25% stiffening when inclusions occupy 10% of the volume. Here we introduce a composite of phase-separated DNA droplets that occupy <10% of an entangled actin network, yet stiffen it 25-fold, reversibly. Microscopy reveals that actin penetrates the DNA droplets, leading network elasticity to determine their size; thus the system exhibits reciprocal control between matrix and droplet properties. We attribute the extraordinary stiffening to entrainment of actin by the droplets, which enlarges the effective inclusions until their contact network dominates the mechanics. This shows that liquid-liquid phase separation can control not only local compositions, but also mechanics, achieving exceptional stiffening at modest filler fractions through local geometries that constrain the matrix beyond the inclusions themselves.
authors: Sam Wilken, Austin Hopkins, Kyu Hwan Choi, John Berezney, Matthew E. Helgeson, M. Cristina Marchetti, Sho Takatori, Zvonimir Dogic, Omar A. Saleh
