title: Room-temperature light-state structure of the AsLOV2-Rac1 optogenetic actuator by sheet-on-sheet serial femtosecond crystallography

abstract: Live-cell imaging of cellular and tissue samples relies predominantly on optical modalities, such as fluorescence, confocal, and multiphoton microscopy, in which cellular information is encoded in emitted photons. Photons scatter and attenuate in biological samples, restricting depth resolution, while the excitation light required to produce them induces photodamage that perturbs the very biology under observation. Magnetic fields, by contrast, traverse biological samples without attenuation at cellular length scales, but the imaging modality that extracts the encoded information, magnetic resonance imaging, cannot resolve individual cells. Here we present Quantum Cell Monitoring (QCM), a widefield nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry platform that encodes single-cell information in stray magnetic fields rather than emitted photons and reads it out at subcellular resolution. Integrated with a specialized live-cell incubator, QCM tracks magnetically labeled living cancer for up to 72 h through their individual magnetic field signatures. It captures single-cell mitosis and morphological remodeling, as well as cell cluster formation, splitting, and migration even within dense regions where brightfield contrast collapses. By shifting the carrier of single-cell information from propagating optical photons to static magnetic stray fields, QCM decouples cell from cellular optical accessibility and auto-fluorescence, enabling sustained live-cell observation in regimes inaccessible to optical microscopy.
authors: Andre Pointner, Sarah Belasi, Regine Schneider-Stock, Roland Nagy
title: Multi-day single-cell magnetic imaging of living cancer cells using Quantum Cell Monitoring

abstract: Filaments are incredible material building blocks that, when entangled together, form robust structures with remarkable adaptive mechanics, from stiff cables to stretchable knits. Basic questions about the mechanism that holds together such structures, especially assemblies like rope, without attractive physical or chemical bonds between constituents are among the oldest considered in materials science. Contradicting a long-standing picture that structural integrity of rope-like assemblies rely on a combination of external loading and inter-filament friction to prevent spontaneous detangling (e.g. fraying of a cut rope), we demonstrate that assemblies of intrinsically-curved filaments can achieve structural integrity purely from the competition of elastic forces that resist shape-change and (traction-free) repulsive forces that prevent overlap. We analyze a friction-free model of assembly of intrinsically-helical filaments, and show that depending on filament number and preferred filament shape, overcrowding in the assemblies generate elastic pre-stresses that give rise to either self-locking entanglement or spontaneous detanglement through propagation of a soliton-like detanglement front through assemblies. We test a generalized fracture criterion for spontaneous detangling and confirm the role of shape-elastic costs to self-locking via experiment and simulation of frictional filaments, demonstrating a range of bundled structures which cannot be made self-locking for any value of friction. The mechanism of ``purely elastic cohesion" illuminated here sheds light on self-locking in a broader class of entangled structures, and further, offers design principles for new classes of active filament materials capable of stimuli-responsive assembly and disassembly.
authors: Benjamin R. Greenvall, Jay van den Berg, Ross E. Meinhart, Patrick A. Staudenmayer, Alfred J. Crosby, Gregory M. Grason
title: No friction required: Self-locking in entangled assemblies of curved filaments

abstract: Swarmalators are particles which have internal degrees of freedom in the form of phase oscillators that can synchronize and change the dynamics of the particles. We explore the active matter disk swarmalator model proposed by Adorjáni [Phys. Rev. E 109, 024607 (2024)] where there is an additional attraction or repulsion determined by whether the phases of particles within a certain radius synchronize or anti-synchronize. This model in the absence of swarmalator rules forms a motility-induced phase-separated (MIPS) state at high activity, but when the swarmalator rules are present, a number of additional states appear including an active gel, labyrinth state, frustrated MIPS, and frustrated fluid states. Here we examine ratchet effects for the Adorjáni model coupled to asymmetric substrates. We find that swarmalator interactions can strongly enhance or suppress active matter ratcheting depending on the structural state of the system, and show that the ratchet efficiency depends on the substrate strength, substrate lattice spacing, and the motor force on the particles. The gel state exhibits the weakest ratcheting for small substrate spacing and can even produce a reversed ratchet motion, but shows the strongest ratcheting for large motor forces. The labyrinth state exhibits the strongest ratcheting over a wide range of parameters since the quasi-one-dimensional labyrinth morphology can match the substrate geometry well.
authors: B. Albert, A. Libal, C. J. O. Reichhardt, C. Reichhardt
title: Ratchet Effects for Swarmalators on Asymmetric Substrates

abstract: Dynamical coarse-graining of neural networks gives macroscopic observables and enables training to be predicted, and controlled in a state space far smaller than the parameter space. In this paper, we first define the learning operator following the training law of neural networks and establish a descent theorem for the learning operator, which serves to determine whether the operator is sufficient to characterize the learning dynamics. Then the exact closure theorem and the dynamic coarse-graining theorem are presented in sequence. The three theorems established in this paper provide a systematic framework for constructing and assessing dynamical coarse-grained models of neural-network training. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of the theorems with a finite-width nonlinear ReLU network. Its dynamic coarse-grained model for a fixed pattern is exactly derived and composed of five independent moments. The model exactly predict the training outputs and evolving learning operator. The framework may also guide the development of approximate coarse-grained models for more general neural networks when exact closure is unavailable.
authors: Lin-Juan Wang, Da Li, Huiling Duan, Jianxiang Wang
title: Dynamical coarse-graining of neural-network training

abstract: Enabled by their controllable optical anisotropy, liquid crystals form a cornerstone of linear optical and display technologies. Bringing the versatile platform into the nonlinear regime, we explore its nonlinear optical anisotropy by high-order harmonic generation spectroscopy. Through a comprehensive study targeting gas, liquid, nematic, and crystalline phases, we present a semi-empirical tight-binding approach that provides insight into the intermolecular character of ultrafast light-driven electron dynamics across soft-matter mesophases. We demonstrate how intermolecular electron hybridization enables spectroscopic access to structural properties, such as the nematic director and order parameter. Outlining such foundational mechanisms opens avenues towards nonlinear liquid crystal devices and ultrafast soft-matter spectroscopies.
authors: Simon Vendelbo Bylling Jensen, Marta L. Murillo-Sánchez, Andrea Annunziata, Angel Rubio, Laura Cattaneo, Nicolas Tancogne-Dejean
title: Theoretical description of high-harmonic spectroscopy for uniaxial nematic and isotropic liquid crystals

abstract: by Lakshay Jain, Omid Noorikalkhoran, Elfriede Derrer-Merk, Bruno Merk Long-term disposal and management of nuclear waste is one of the major hurdles for nuclear energy. Deep geological disposal, an idea originating in the 1970s, is currently the preferred path being followed in many countries. However, acceptance of this approach is hindered by societal concerns around the safety of the “one-million years” geological disposal and passing the waste burden to future generations. iMAGINE, an integrated nuclear system based on molten salt fast reactor technology with self-sustained iso-breeding, online clean-up and reverse reprocessing, has been proposed as an innovative way to eliminate the demand for a long-term high-level waste disposal. In this work, we investigate the use of iMAGINE as a technological approach for reimagining high-level nuclear waste management by overcoming the challenges of classical partitioning and transmutation (P&T). After discussing the current status and limitations of P&T along with an overview of the nuclear waste classification and management framework existing in major nuclear power producing countries, we demonstrate the potential impact of iMAGINE in simplifying the disposal of high-level waste. The results indicate that among the key long-lived radionuclides, many lie well below the criteria for requiring deep geological disposal. Besides Finland, India and Russia where most (or all) of the important long-lived fission products exceed current high-level waste thresholds, only two to three fission products (generally with half-lives from 30 to 100 years) exceed the national limits in Canada, China, France, Germany, Japan, and South Korea, while concrete conclusions can’t be drawn for the UK and US based on available information. The results presented here do not aim to make inflated claims but should be seen as the scientific basis for deeper discussions amongst all nuclear waste disposal stakeholders to explore a novel technological solution for rethinking high-level waste management and possibly eliminating the need for a “one-million years” geological disposal.
authors: Lakshay Jain, Omid Noorikalkhoran, Elfriede Derrer-Merk, Bruno Merk
title: Rethinking deep geological disposal: Opportunities for reimagining nuclear waste management created through iMAGINE

abstract: Particle-filled soft composites generally stiffen as particle loading increases, imposing a trade-off between functionality and compliance. Here, we show that this trade-off can be overcome by designing particles to actively direct gelation rather than act as passive fillers. In a sol-rich elastomer matrix, sol-phase kinetics redirect network formation towards particle-mediated assembly, yielding anomalous softening despite increasing particle content. This response is governed by topological reconfiguration of the load-bearing network during gelation rather than by filler loading alone. A structure-based model captures the composition-dependent onset of this behaviour, and the same response is reproduced across distinct particle systems. The resulting materials combine functionality with softness, energy dissipation, and recoverability under large deformation. These findings establish topology-guided gelation as a general strategy for engineering compliant functional composites for soft robotic actuation, conformal interfaces, and other systems that require both deformability and embedded material functionality.
authors: Yonghyun Cho, Hyeongho Min, Hongdeok Kim, Dongeun Lee, Minjune Kim, Siyeon Jang, Ali Amini, Zitang Wei, Hosub Lim, Hwan-ho Cho, Bo-yong Park, Sang Won Lee, Joonmyung Choi, Metin Sitti, Sangyul Baik
title: Rigid Particle-Induced Anomalous Softening in Elastomer Composites

abstract: Synchronization with vibrating boundaries can qualitatively alter the dynamics of confined granular fluids and control the collision-induced transfer of energy to horizontal motion. We develop an Enskog kinetic theory for the active phase of a driven granular monolayer within the framework of the $Δ$-model, which accounts for the transfer of energy from the vertical to the horizontal degrees of freedom of grains. Synchronization effects are incorporated through a state-dependent effective collision rule governed by the interplay between the local collision frequency and a characteristic synchronization time. A viscous drag force is also included to account for energy dissipation arising from interactions with the confining plates. Within this framework, we characterize the homogeneous active state and use it as the reference state for a Chapman--Enskog expansion. The solution of the Enskog equation to Navier--Stokes order then yields explicit expressions for the shear and bulk viscosities, the thermal conductivity, the diffusive heat coefficient, and the first-order contribution to the cooling rate, consistently accounting for inelasticity, damping, finite-density effects, and synchronization. Event-driven molecular-dynamics simulations show that the theory accurately describes the steady temperature and shear and bulk viscosities over a broad region of the active phase. Close to the discontinuous synchronization-controlled absorbing transition, deviations are mainly attributed to the mean-field coarse-graining of the microscopic synchronization dynamics: fluctuations of the collision-dependent injection amplitude and correlations between synchronization and pre-collisional velocities become increasingly important. These results provide a kinetic description of synchronization-controlled transport and delineate its range of validity near the absorbing transition.
authors: David González Méndez, Rubén Gómez González, Raphaël Maire, Vicente Garzó, Ignacio Pagonabarraga
title: Synchronization-controlled transport near an absorbing transition: Effective Enskog kinetic theory of a driven granular monolayer

abstract: Active droplets provide a platform for converting microscopic propulsion into macroscopic flow. Previous realizations of bacteria-driven droplet rotation typically rely on nearby solid boundaries, external fields, or dense active nematics. Here, we report autonomous rotation of droplets in a three-dimensional aqueous two-phase system driven by interfacial population of \textit{Pseudomonas aeruginosa}. Combining confocal microscopy with fluid particle dynamics simulations, we show that amphiphilic bacteria accumulate at the dextran--polyethylene glycol interface and preferentially move and orient along the local tangent. Interfacial localization partitions the force-free swimming dipole between the two liquid phases, allowing either phase to experience a finite active torque while the combined system remains torque balanced. The simulated interfacial population is more spatially heterogeneous than in the experiments, emphasizing that both the bacterial distribution and its signed orientational organization can influence the instantaneous torque. Over the accessible size range, the macroscopic angular velocity exhibits an inverse-radius ($R^{-1}$) dependence. We also formulate a theoretical model to rationalize this scaling law, revealing how the macroscopic rotation is governed by collective interfacial swimming and surface coverage. These results identify a fluid-interface-mediated route for converting swimmer activity into macroscopic rotational flow and establish a strategy for harnessing interfacial active matter to regulate droplet dynamics.
authors: Dixi Yang, Anheng Wang, Chunming Wang, Hajime Tanaka, Jiaxing Yuan
title: Interfacial bacteria-driven rotation of free-floating active droplets

abstract: Learning molecular models of RNA requires simulation data that capture conformational variability and provide consistent physical training signals. Here, we introduce mdRNAcat, a curated dataset of all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of 48 RNA systems selected to promote sequence diversity. Each system is simulated using replica-exchange with solute scaling (REST2), with 32 Hamiltonian states and production lengths of 200-300 ns per state. The dataset provides atomic coordinates, instantaneous forces, and forces reevaluated under the unscaled reference Hamiltonian, together with structural annotations and replica-exchange metadata. Coordinates and forces are available at 1 ps intervals for the reference state and 100 ps intervals across all states in a standardized HDF5 format. We characterize conformational sampling, exchange behavior, base pairing, and sugar-pucker distributions to document the properties of the simulated ensembles. mdRNAcat provides a reusable resource for developing and evaluating data-driven RNA models, including coarse-grained force fields.
authors: Anton E. Dorn, Emile de Bruyn, Fabrice von der Lehr, Philipp Knechtges, Stefan Kesselheim, Alexander Schug
title: mdRNAcat: A Molecular Dynamics RNA Catalog of REST2 Conformational Ensembles

abstract: Insect exoskeletons abruptly acquire complex three-dimensional forms during metamorphosis from larva to pupa. This transformation occurs through the unfolding of preformed wrinkle structures inside the larval body under internal pressure. Inspired by this process, we investigate an inverse-origami strategy for fabricating curved surfaces. Whereas conventional origami produces three-dimensional objects by folding a flat sheet, this strategy produces curved surfaces by unfolding preformed wrinkle structures. The central design problem is to derive a wrinkle structure from a prescribed target surface. Our key idea is to regard a wrinkle structure as a unidirectional stretching field, which specifies at each point the stretch produced when the structure unfolds. We first derive such a field from the target surface geometry and then translate it into spatially varying wrinkle directions and spacing, so that the wrinkle structure unfolds into the target. The resulting numerical designs approximate the intrinsic metric of the target surface. We demonstrate the method on multiple target surfaces through numerical construction, mechanical unfolding simulations, and 3D-printed prototypes. This work provides a biologically inspired geometric design principle for encoding prescribed surface shapes in wrinkle structures, as well as a framework for designing and fabricating deployable curved surfaces.
authors: Kentaro Morikawa, Yuuki Shimizu, Nen Saito, Yasuhiro Inoue
title: Inverse origami inspired by insect morphogenesis: geometric design of wrinkle structures for curved surface formation

abstract: The intrinsic ability of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), such as the {beta}2-adrenergic receptor ({beta}2AR), to sample an ensemble of distinct conformational states with varying affinities and catalytic activities for intracellular transducers such as G proteins and {beta} arrestins is a feature that underlies their signaling complexity. The structural features of the full ensemble of accessible conformations remain largely inaccessible to conventional biophysical techniques due to the low populations of transient or intermediate states. Here, we integrate pressure-resolved double electron electron resonance (PR DEER) with the ProGuide biased molecular dynamics framework to map elusive {beta}2AR conformations obscured under ambient conditions. Our results demonstrate a pressure dependent, global two-state equilibrium between inactive- and active-like conformations in the unliganded receptor and indicate a high degree of allosteric coupling among transmembrane helices in the absence of ligand binding. Notably, {beta}2AR bound to the superagonist BI 167107 samples a smaller conformational space than the unliganded active conformation revealed by pressure, suggesting that this agonist constrains {beta}2AR to a more restricted subset of conformers within the active ensemble. This finding points towards a conformational selection mechanism of activation of the {beta}2AR wherein signaling variability exists because of conformational heterogeneity within the active state.
authors: Lerch, M.; Brennan, P. C.; Garces, A. M.; Grosskopf, J. D.; Pani, B.
title: Unliganded Active State of the β2-Adrenergic Receptor Revealed by Pressure-Resolved DEER and ProGuide Molecular Modeling

abstract: Hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) provides powerful insight into protein structure and dynamics, but interpretation of protection patterns at atomic resolution often requires complementary computational modeling. We present PHENOMS, an open-source Python package that integrates molecular dynamics trajectories with HDX-MS data to analyze backbone hydrogen-bond networks by tracking how individual hydrogen bonds and residue-residue contacts form, break, and reorganize throughout the simulations. This residue-level analysis can reveal local structural changes that may be missed by conventional global trajectory metrics. PHENOMS employs a multithreaded, Rust-accelerated computational engine that achieved an average 16-fold speedup (up to 100-fold) over widely used Python-based MD analysis packages in our benchmarks, while retaining individual hydrogen-bond resolution in every trajectory frame. We demonstrate PHENOMS through multiple retrospective case studies using published and in-house datasets, showing that it can recapitulate HDX-MS protection patterns, identify key residues that drive coordinated structural changes, and benchmark the computational efficiency of the approach. With automated quality-control workflows, PHENOMS provides a framework for integrating hydrogen-bond analysis with HDX-MS data or serves as a standalone, high-throughput tool for analyzing MD trajectories for broader applications in protein engineering, drug discovery, and structural biology.
authors: Novy, B.; Lin, S.-H.; Dey, R.; Temple, B.; Hajicek, N.; Petrotchenko, E. V.; Borchers, C. H.; Sondek, J.; Popov, K. I.
title: PHENOMS: Open-Source Software for Rust-Accelerated Hydrogen-Bond Analysis in Molecular Dynamics Simulations

abstract: Time-resolved serial synchrotron crystallography (TR-SSX) has become a powerful approach for investigating structural dynamics in proteins under near-physiological conditions. Its successful application, however, depends on robust sample delivery, reliable pump-probe synchronization, and reproducible data-processing strategies. Here, an injector-based pump-probe TR-SSX workflow at the MicroMAX beamline is applied to investigate the structural dynamics of the LOV1 domain of the blue-light photoreceptor phototropin from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (CrPhotLOV1). Room-temperature serial datasets were collected for an independently measured laser-off dark state together with four light-activated pump-probe time windows (0-350, 500-850, 1000-1350 and 1500-1850 {micro}s after a microsecond laser pulse). All four time windows and an interleaved pump-probe dark reference were recorded in a single run with the JUNGFRAU detector at 2 kHz. Because thioether adduct formation in CrPhotLOV1 is complete within about 20 {micro}s and the adduct persists for hundreds of seconds, the four delays probe the same photoadduct state and serve as independent replicates. The workflow was evaluated in terms of data quality, light contamination in the pump-probe dark reference, difference Fourier analysis, extrapolated electron-density maps and refinement of light-state models. Consistent activation levels were obtained across all time points, enabling reliable structural interpretation of the light-activated state. Difference Fourier maps and refined extrapolated models reproducibly revealed formation of the characteristic FMN-Cys57 thioether adduct together with localized rearrangements within the chromophore-binding pocket. The refined light-state structures agree closely with previously reported CrPhotLOV1 models. These results establish a robust and reproducible workflow for injector-based pump-probe TR-SSX at the MicroMAX beamline, suitable for routine time-resolved studies of light-responsive proteins.
authors: Olasz, B.; Wisniewska, M.; Koczurowska, A.; Casadei, C. M.; Solecka, A.; Kapetanaki, S. M.; Pachota, M.; Lopes Cavalcante, L.; Asghar, A.; Lang, D.; Milas, M.; Ursby, T.; Shankar, M. K.; Chenchiliyan, M.; Nan, J.; Nogly, P.
title: Injector-based pump-probe serial synchrotron crystallography of CrPhotLOV1 at the MicroMAX beamline

abstract: Fluorophore concentration measures and local histogram entropy describe different aspects of endogenous fluorophore maps. We investigate whether their combination improves discrimination between normal and cancerous lung tissue and which features contribute to predictions. Chemometric fluorescence microscopy (CFM) provides concentration maps of tryptophan, elastin, reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH), and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD). A neural network based on generalized additive models with structured interactions (GAMI-Net) is used to compare concentration-only, entropy-only, and combined representations through explicit main effects and pairwise interactions. The mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUCs) across five-fold cross-validation were $95.9\% \pm 0.7\%$, $96.4\% \pm 1.6\%$, and $98.4\% \pm 0.7\%$, respectively; variability is reported as standard deviation (SD). Their aggregate differences are consistent with the hypothesis of complementary predictive information. FAD entropy, NADH concentration, and NADH entropy were the leading main effects in the combined model. The learned log-odds contributions include a U-shaped elastin-entropy relationship and nonmonotonic tryptophan relationships. By exposing how concentration and entropy enter predictions, this interpretable framework turns label-free fluorescence classification into specific, testable hypotheses about tissue metabolism and extracellular-matrix organization, motivating specimen-grouped and external validation.
authors: Yin, Z.; Xu, M.; Virany, L.; GUO, Y.
title: Interpretable Deep Learning of Endogenous Fluorophore Concentration and Entropy for Lung Tissue Classification

abstract: Living systems move loads with agents that pull against one another. Kinesin and dynein pull one vesicle, ants haul a dead insect, and antagonist muscles move a joint. Whether the timing of the forces can, by itself, determine which side moves the load is not well understood. Here, combining experiments, theory, and simulations of a tug-of-war between two matched teams of spring-coupled robots, we show that the relative timing of the pull forces breaks the symmetry and decides the contest. Teams pulling in unison or in strict alternation tie. Between these, the lagging team wins, most strongly near a quarter cycle, because the springs unload while the leading team coasts and the lagging team still pulls. In the model and in robot simulations, braking rather than coasting between pulls, once strong enough, shifts the advantage to the leading team. Winning and losing leave distinct signatures in each robot's motor current. Using these local signals, we formulate an embodied decentralized phase-adaptation rule that enables transient leadership to switch between teams, allowing the collective to transport high-friction cargo and to navigate around obstacles towards a prescribed target without explicit communication.
authors: Chatterjee, A.; Srisuchinnawong, A.; Manoonpong, P.; Bhamla, S.
title: Embodied timing turns a robotic tug-of-war into cooperative transport

title: Environment-specific virtual head direction representation in the human anteroventral thalamus during memory-guided spatial orientation

abstract: Selective pharmacological control of gap junction communication remains challenging because existing small-molecule connexin inhibitors act across multiple isoforms. The structural basis of this broad activity remains incompletely understood. Here, we used single-particle cryo-electron microscopy to examine native connexin-46/50 gap junction channels treated with two commonly used and chemically distinct inhibitors, 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB) and carbenoxolone (CBX). Both treatments perturb the hydrophobic N-terminal (NT)-docking groove, but produce distinct conformational ensembles. 2-APB yields ordered destabilized-open and gated NT states resembling conformations observed during physiological pH- and Ca2+-dependent gating, with ligand- and lipid-associated densities accompanying the gated state. In contrast, CBX-compatible density occupies the same groove and is associated with loss of an ordered NT conformation, consistent with steric competition and altered physicochemical complementarity at the NT-docking site. Comparison with inhibitor-treated connexin-32 and connexin-36 structures identifies this region as a structurally conserved, pharmacologically sensitive pocket. These findings reveal how chemically diverse inhibitors perturb a conserved element of the native gating machinery while producing divergent NT-gating ensembles, providing a structural rationale for broad cross-isoform activity and identifying sequence-variable pocket margins that may support more selective modulation.
authors: Jarodsky, J. M.; Myers, J. B.; Reichow, S. L.
title: Distinct modes of N-terminal remodeling through a conserved inhibitor pocket in connexin-46/50

abstract: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most frequent mRNA modification in eukaryotic cells and is involved in the regulation of gene expression. Since viruses can hijack the host machinery to perform this chemical editing, m6A is also involved in viral replication and innate immune system activation. Nowadays only few m6A viral maps are available, making complementary methods crucial to accelerate the investigation of these mechanisms. Here we propose MEMAR, a Maximum Entropy model, to predict the methylation frequency, depending on the eight-mers nucleotide motif surrounding the central adenosine. MEMAR is a fast, simple and modular model: it can be trained on human methylation maps and refined including the methylation level per transcript and the position of motifs relatively to the coding regions. This modularity allows strong adaptability, leading MEMAR to better perform over influenza A segments than the mammalian state-of-the-art DeepSRAMP method. MEMAR generalization potential is assessed on i) human transcripts from GLORI and miCLIP experiments ii) HEK293T and HeLa cell lines iii) positive and negative influenza A viral segments and iv) altered-methylation experiments. A two-state dynamical model between m6A writers and erasers explains MEMAR predictive power as a function of the global methylation percentage, and allows us to interpret anomalies in altered conditions through variations of methylation or de-methylation binding constants.
authors: Lecce, I.; Brun, P.-G.; Cocco, S.
title: A maximum entropy model for m6A prediction: from human transcripts to influenza A viral segments

abstract: Macrophages are essential cells of the innate immune system that regulate wound healing and tissue homeostasis. They exert diverse functions, depending on their polarization state, which can lead to either functional healing of the tissue or fibrosis. Macrophage polarization state is affected by both the local biochemical and mechanical microenvironment within the tissue, suggesting a possible dependence of macrophage function on cell mechanical state, which has been poorly explored to date. In this study, we provide a systematic and quantitative characterization of the viscoelastic properties of unstimulated, pro-inflammatory, and anti-inflammatory monocyte-derived primary human macrophages at the single-cell level using atomic force microscopy. Pro-inflammatory macrophages exhibited a lower elastic modulus (E = 458.8 {+/-} 179.9 Pa) and a more dissipative response (low frequency exponent = 0.22 {+/-} 0.03) than anti-inflammatory macrophages (E = 716 {+/-} 345.6 Pa and  = 0.15 {+/-} 0.04). These differences in mechanical properties were independent of cell morphology but correlated with differences in podosome distribution with pro-inflammatory macrophages exhibiting a dispersed distribution, and anti-inflammatory macrophages a more clustered distribution. This study identifies polarization-dependent mechanical differences in human primary macrophages and provides a quantitative experimental framework for future work in macrophage mechanobiology.
authors: El Showk, H.; Lunardi, C.; Erkan, R.; Kurniawan, N. A. A.; Smits, A.; Angeloni, L.
title: Polarization affects viscoelasticity and podosome distribution of primary human macrophages

abstract: Animals that acquire a microbial symbiont from the environment must find it against an overwhelming background of other bacteria. The bobtail squid Euprymna recruits its luminous symbiont Vibrio fischeri from seawater in which the symbiont occurs at fewer than ten cells per millilitre, and the host is transcriptionally primed for colonisation as soon as the first handful of symbionts become detectable at the light organ, too few to signal directly and implying a detection event upstream of it. We hypothesised that the paired olfactory organs, which sit at the entrance to the mantle cavity and hence in the path of all inhaled water, are that site. Here we characterise cilia-driven flow, particle capture and neuronal activity at the olfactory organ in hatchlings of Euprymna scolopes and E. berryi and in three non-symbiotic cuttlefish and squid species, i.e. species with no known light-organ symbiosis. In Euprymna the organ is a densely ciliated, mucus-coated epithelium packed with putative chemosensory cells and expressing the peptidoglycan-recognition receptor EsPGRP4, and its motile cilia drive a vortical flow that converges head-on onto the sensory face and persists to at least 96 h after hatching, independent of colonization status. Suspended beads accumulate there more strongly than at the light organ, and swimming symbionts follow the same flow yet are retained an order of magnitude more strongly than inert beads of the same size. Cells within the organ show spontaneous calcium transients, and the subset of cells and the firing rate change in response to waterborne stimuli, including live V. fischeri. In the three non-symbiotic species the equivalent organ sweeps water past its face rather than onto it, confining capture to the margins. Taken together, these findings suggest that in Euprymna the olfactory organ may concentrate, hold and detect arriving bacteria at a chemosensory surface before they reach the light organ.
authors: Porcella, G.; Nawroth, J. C.
title: Cilia-driven fluid vortices deliver symbiotic bacteria onto the mucociliary olfactory organ of the bobtail squid

abstract: Voltage-gated Potassium channels (Kv channels) comprise twelve subfamilies found in the human genome. They demonstrate diversified activation behaviors, represented by the varied shapes of activation currents, which are usually modeled by individual kinetic schemes of many parameters that make channel comparisons difficult. Here, we present a minimal-state kinetic model, aiming to compare different Kv channel activation currents by a unified model system. By omitting the short-lived transient states and neglecting the detailed transition pathways, this model employs only minimal significant states necessary to approximate the activation currents. Few model-parameters are used that capture the varied current-features, leading to a convenient comparison among Kv channels. In addition, this model incorporates a gating factor, which accurately represents the channel opening event upon applying a voltage pulse. A special feature of the model is its adaptability via simple modifications, that any channel-dependent kinetic scheme can be easily incorporated into this model framework, helping develop exact channel mechanisms.
authors: Wu, D.; Jiang, S.; Huang, Y.
title: Characterizing features of Kv channel activation currents by a minimal-state kinetic model

abstract: Protein purification is a fundamental step for analyzing individual proteins and protein complexes and identifying interactions with other proteins, DNA, or RNA. A variety of protein purification strategies exist to address desired scale, throughput, and downstream applications. However, selecting an effective experimental procedure remains a largely empirical process that a quick literature review can help guide. Researchers typically survey on the order of a dozen publications for proteins with similar biochemical properties, assessing conditions on a case-by-case basis, leaving no systematic framework for comparison and decision-making at the scale of entire protein families. As protein engineering and design evolve, identifying effective purification conditions remains critical for obtaining sufficient quantities of properly folded and functional proteins. To address this gap, we developed ProtoPure, an LLM-based workflow and database that automates the extraction, standardization and analysis of protein purification conditions from peer-reviewed literature at scale. Given a user-defined UniProt table-enabling flexible selection of proteins by family, organism, or proteome. ProtoPure retrieves associated publications, classifies them based on the presence of purification protocols, and extracts a standardized set of 12 purification parameters (e.g., buffer composition, elution conditions). By transforming dispersed experimental descriptions into a structured resource, ProtoPure makes it possible to compare purification strategies across thousands of proteins. The resulting dataset revealed quantitative convergence toward a limited set of recombinant expression practices, with BL21(DE3)-based systems dominating protein production and recurrent combinations of expression host, inducer, growth medium, and plasmid occurring substantially more frequently than expected by chance. In contrast, downstream purification parameters exhibited greater diversity, revealing a workflow architecture that combines standardized expression infrastructure with more flexible biochemical components.

title: ProtoPure: Literature Mining and Analysis of Protein Purification Protocols at Proteome Scale

abstract: Fast endophilin-mediated endocytosis (FEME) relies on the coordinated activities of membrane-remodeling proteins and multivalent protein interaction networks. Endophilin is a potent membrane curvature generator through its N-BAR domain and forms multivalent interactions with the proline-rich motifs (PRMs) of lamellipodin via its SH3 domain. Although these interactions are known to promote biomolecular condensation, their functional consequences for membrane remodeling have remained unclear. Here, we investigate how SH3/PRM mediated phase separation regulates endophilin-driven membrane curvature generation. Using purified recombinant proteins, giant unilamellar vesicles, quantitative fluorescence microscopy, and in vitro phase separation assays, we show that multivalent interactions between endophilin and lamellipodin drive the formation of membrane-associated protein-rich phases that strongly suppress endophilin mediated membrane tubulation. Competitive disruption of SH3/PRM interactions with the synaptojanin-derived peptide PP19 (containing only two PRM motifs) rapidly dissolves condensates and restores membrane curvature generation without affecting the intrinsic curvature-generating activity of endophilin. We further demonstrate that this regulatory mechanism is conserved across endophilin A1, A2, and A3 isoforms and depends critically on interaction valency: a multivalent PRM7 construct recapitulates condensate formation and curvature suppression, whereas mono or divalent PRM constructs does not. Together, these findings identify multivalent SH3/PRM interactions as a reversible molecular switch that balances biomolecular condensation and membrane remodeling. Multiple mechanisms, including post-translational modifications, likely regulate the multivalency of these interactions. Our results thus establish a broad functional link between protein phase separation and membrane mechanics, providing a framework for understanding how multivalent interaction networks regulate membrane shaping in multiple endocytic pathways.
authors: Baumgart, T.; Bullock, O. L.; Manjunatha, A.; James, H. P.
title: Multivalency in endocytic accessory proteins orchestrates membrane shape transitions

abstract: Intercalating dyes are widely used to visualize DNA in single-molecule experiments, but their effects on DNA-processing proteins remain incompletely characterized. Here, we study the effects of intercalators on DNA loop extrusion by SMC complexes. Intercalating dyes become fluorescent upon DNA binding, enabling direct visualization of extruded DNA loops. As dye intercalation alters the biophysical properties of DNA by lengthening and unwinding it, we examine how that modifies loop extrusion. We systematically characterize the effects of intercalators, and find that they stiffen DNA, partly neutralize its charge, and can substantially reduce the binding and ATPase activity of SMCs. We assess four dyes and conclude that SYBR Gold and SYTOX Orange are less invasive intercalators than SYTOX Green or YOYO-1. While loop extrusion is qualitatively not affected by intercalation, quantitative values for SMC binding and looping rates differ significantly from those in the absence of intercalators. We present a new dye-free loop-extrusion assay (utilizing local fluorescent spots along DNA), and find that loop extrusion proceeds at 1.75{+/-}0.26 kb/s for S. cerevisiae condensin without dyes, while adding intercalators leads to a two-fold lower rate. Our findings establish that intercalators quantitatively modify loop extrusion parameters, and we offer practical recommendations for minimizing their impact.
authors: Analikwu, B. T.; van der Torre, J.; Dekker, C.
title: Intercalator effects on DNA loop extrusion by SMC proteins

abstract: Nanosecond pulse electric fields (nsPEFs) are an established treatment modality for cancer and have emerged as a potential approach for deep brain stimulation and cardiac defibrillation. The concerns in these two applications are at odds. While pulsed-field electroporation applications aim to minimise excitation of surrounding neurons, therapies based on neuronal stimulation demand minimal electroporation of neurons. Although nsPEFs offer various advantages, such as minimising power input and suppressing electrode reactions, they require strong electric fields to reach both the excitation and electroporation thresholds, so maintaining a safety gap between the two is crucial. Because these coupled processes unfold on time scales ranging from nanoseconds to milliseconds and cannot be resolved simultaneously in experiments, a computational approach is used. This study examines the interplay between excitation and electroporation within the Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) framework for a planar two-bilayer model coupled with the Asymptotic Smoluchowski Equation for electroporation, and solves for transmembrane potentials (TMPs), pore statistics and pore size evolution. The model can predict the role of electroporation in modulating neuronal responses and qualitatively explain key experimental observations in the literature. These include excitation with a single action potential (SAP), repetitive spiking (RS), and depolarisation block (DB), and are explained here with detailed mechanisms, including the subtle effects of strong electric fields and electroporating currents on ion-channel dynamics. Importantly, our work establishes a parameter space for strength-duration curves in regimes of safe excitation without electroporation, and vice versa. For a neuron with an equivalent RC time constant of 10 ns, pulses shorter than about 20 ns electroporate the membrane before they excite it, and the safety factor falls below 5% for 1-ns pulses. The work also expands into s and ms pulses, and delves into possible regimes that could lead to neuronal inviability due to irreversible electroporation or excessive fractional pore area.
authors: FARIDI, M. R. A.; Manchanda, R.; Thaokar, R. M.
title: Dynamical regimes of excitable cells under pulsed electric fields: From excitation to electroporation

abstract: Focal adhesions mechanically couple the actomyosin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix (ECM), contributing to mechanosensing and mechanical homeostasis. They span diverse states in response to the mechanical environment, from nascent adhesions and focal complexes to mature and supermature adhesions, undergoing dynamic remodeling. However, how ECM-dependent force generation and internal mechanoadaptation jointly shape the emergence and stability of these states remains unclear. Here, we develop a four-variable dynamical model comprising adhesion state, transmitted force, reinforcement activity, and an adaptive mechanical stress target. As ECM stiffness varies, the model generates distinct modes while regulating mechanical stress toward this target. The force-response timescale further modifies the stability structure, giving rise to a stable oscillatory mode. Within multistable regimes, adhesion-mode selection depends not only on current ECM stiffness but also on its history. These results show that diverse adhesion modes can emerge from a common mechanoadaptive system, with ECM stiffness history influencing mode selection.
authors: Matsumoto, E.; Deguchi, S.
title: Mechanoadaptive focal adhesion-actomyosin coupling organizes diverse modes across ECM stiffness

abstract:
Transcription factors (TFs) regulate gene expression by binding to specific genomic loci determined by DNA sequence. Their sequence specificity is commonly summarized by a consensus binding motif. However, eukaryotic genomes contain billions of low-affinity DNA sequences to which TFs associate with a sequence-dependent binding energy. We currently lack insight into how the genomic sequence defines this spectrum of binding energies and the resulting pattern of TF localization. Here, we set out to obtain a quantitative understanding of sequence-dependent TF binding to both motif and nonmotif sequences. We achieve this by first pursuing accurate measurements of physical binding energies of human TF Krüppel-like factor 4 (Klf4) to a library of short DNA sequences in a fluorescence-anisotropy-based bulk competitive binding assay. abstract: Spontaneous phospholipid flip-flop sets the background against which flippases, floppases, and scramblases create and dissipate membrane asymmetry. How the associated free-energy barrier depends on lipid chemistry and on the surrounding membrane remains unclear, because experiments are few and contradictory and previous simulations covered only a small part of the lipidome. Here, we calculate Martini 3 flip-flop free-energy barriers for over 700 membrane--lipid combinations, the largest such dataset to our knowledge. A systematic single component bilayer panel of five headgroups, three linkages, and 35 tail families is complemented by mixed bilayers, from binary mixtures to organelle-inspired compositions, that place the same lipid in different membranes and thus separate the effects of lipid chemistry and the membrane environment. In single component bilayers, the barrier rises with tighter tail packing and depends strongly on headgroup and tail unsaturation but only weakly on linkage. Moving a lipid into a mixed bilayer shifts its barrier as much as most headgroup substitutions do, and the shift follows the change in local tail order. Within a shared membrane, headgroup differences are mostly smaller than between single component bilayers, so part of a headgroup effect arises from the membrane that the lipid forms. A Bayesian model combining chemical descriptors with local membrane structure predicts barriers for withheld lipid families and membranes with cross-validated errors of 2.8 and 3.8 kJ/mol. The calculated trends agree qualitatively with native-lipid vesicle experiments, although Martini 3 underestimates the barrier differences between lipids, gives lower barriers than atomistic models, and overstates the effect of cholesterol.
authors: Vuorte, M. I.; Pandey, U.; Javanainen, M.
title: Structural Determinants of the Energetic Barrier of Phospholipid Flip-Flop
